s:
Assertion (A): A fall in poverty does not necessarily imply a fall in inequality.
Reason (R): Poverty may decline while the distribution of income or consumption becomes more unequal.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true. A reduction in poverty can coexist with rising inequality when gains are distributed unevenly across population groups.
tq: Test whether the reason directly explains the possibility stated in the assertion.

s: Which one of the following is identified as a limitation of consumption-based inequality estimates?
o: They may understate the incomes of the highest-income groups.
They measure only inter-State per capita income gaps.
They necessarily show that inequality is falling.
They exclude all information about poverty.
x: Consumption data may understate the incomes of the top end, thereby affecting the assessment of inequality. Such data do not necessarily measure only inter-State gaps or prove that inequality is declining.
tq: Find the specific limitation and reject absolute claims about what the data necessarily show.
